title: pi-ui WebSocket protocol v1 (spike subset)
description: Frames of the /ws/v1 hub (docs/ws-protocol.md, docs/spike-interfaces.md §6/§7). Self-contained on purpose: server/scripts/gen.sh generates one Go file per schemas/*.json, so a cross-file $ref would produce code that does not compile; the shapes shared with core.json (session id, error code, timestamp) are therefore re-declared here with a Ws prefix. The document root is the union of the client frames, so the hub validates every inbound frame with a single compiled schema; server frames are declared too, because the contract and the tests reason about them. Every object keeps additionalProperties at its default (true), so a frame from a newer client survives unchanged and unknown fields are never a reason to drop a connection; `required` is what the hub enforces, and it is enforced by the generated UnmarshalJSON as well.

WsProtocolVersion.description: Negotiated protocol version, carried by `hello` and echoed by `welcome`. Re-declared from core.json (see the file description); a future v2 ships alongside v1 instead of mutating v1 shapes, and a client that asks for a version the server does not speak is refused before any subscription exists.

WsSessionId.description: Server session id, re-declared from core.json: "s_" plus 16 lowercase hex characters. Every session-scoped frame carries it, so a malformed id is rejected at the validation boundary instead of reaching a handler.

WsEntryId.description: pi session entry id, re-declared from core.json and copied verbatim from the child's entry_appended records. Used as a durable replay cursor when the client has one, because it survives a server restart while seq does not.

WsErrorCode.description: Machine-readable error code, re-declared from core.json's ErrorCode (core.json stays authoritative; internal/ws has a test that fails when the two lists drift). Clients switch on these values, so they are never renamed or reused; clients must also tolerate codes they do not know and degrade to a generic message.

message.description: Human-readable English message, safe to display: never provider secrets, never conversation content. It is a hint for logs and toasts, not a contract — clients branch on code.

details.description: Optional structured context (limit, field, retryAfterMs, ...). Open map so a new detail never breaks a client.

WsError.description: Error object of a failed `response` and of the `server.error` event. Both carry the same shape so a client needs one renderer for every failure.

WsTimestamp.description: RFC3339 timestamp, re-declared from core.json as a pattern instead of "format": "date-time" so codegen keeps it a string. The hub fills it with UTC and milliseconds when the publisher leaves it empty.

name.description: Client name shown in server logs and in the `clients` count diagnostics ("pi-ui-test", "pi-ui-android"). Free-form: the server never branches on it.

version.description: Client version string, for support and diagnostics only. The server compares versions of the protocol (`v`), never of the client.

WsHelloClient.description: Identifying information about the connecting client. Optional client fields beyond these two are preserved but not interpreted.

WsHello.description: First frame of every connection and the only frame accepted before the handshake finishes. The server answers `welcome` (same `v`) or closes with HTTP 4401 when the version is unknown or the peer is not authorized; nothing else is read from the socket until then.

seq.description: Last seq the client already has; replay returns the events of the session with Seq > since.seq. seq 0 means "from the beginning of the ring", which is also what a fresh subscriber sends. Cheap (memory only) but limited to the ring window.

oneOf.description: In-memory cursor: replay everything the ring still holds for the session.

Durable cursor: replay delegates to the injected Replayer (get_entries), which survives a server restart. An unknown cursor yields complete=false plus a replay_cursor_invalid error instead of a silently empty replay.

WsReplayCursor.description: Where a subscriber wants to resume from. Exactly one of the two variants: seq is the cheap in-memory cursor, entryId is the durable one. Both may be absent, which means "only live events". A cursor is a hint, never an authorization: the replay window is bounded by the ring, and the client reloads through REST when it fell out.

replay.description: Opt-out flag for clients that only want the live tail (default true): false suppresses the whole replay sequence, so a background viewer never pays for history it will not render. Subscribing to a session the server does not know is not an error — the server could not tell a race from a bug — and the client learns about a missing session from the REST surface.

WsClientSubscribe.description: Registers the connection as a subscriber of one session. Replay is per subscriber, so two clients resuming from different cursors never see each other's gap.

WsClientUnsubscribe.description: Drops the subscription and the buffered backlog of that session for this connection. Idempotent: unsubscribing twice is not an error, because a client racing with a reconnect must not have to track server state.

id.description: Client-chosen correlation id, echoed in the `response`. The server never generates it for this frame, so the client can pipeline commands; the id is scoped to the connection.

op.description: Dotted operation name (session.prompt, session.steer, session.abort, session.command.raw, ...). Deliberately a pattern and not an enum: ops are registered in one map in internal/sessions and Phase 3 adds entries there, so the schema pins the shape and the server answers an unknown op with a coded error instead of the validation layer rejecting the frame.

payload.description: Op-specific arguments, passed through to the handler verbatim. Untyped on purpose: the payload belongs to the op (and, for session.command.raw, to pi), so pinning it here would force a schema change for every new pi command.

WsClientCommand.description: Asks the server to act on a session. Exactly one `response` with the same id comes back — ok=true with the handler's data, or ok=false with a coded error — so the client always has a terminal outcome to clear its optimistic UI.

id.description: pi request id of the `request` frame being answered, not a client-chosen id. It is forwarded to the child as extension_ui_response.id.

value.description: Answer of a select|input|editor dialog: the chosen option, the typed text or the editor content. Untyped because the value's shape follows the dialog method.

cancelled.description: Explicit dismissal. The server also writes cancelled=true to the child when the dialog times out, so the child always gets exactly one answer.

WsClientUiResponse.description: Answers an extension UI dialog. The first answer wins; later ones get response{ok:false,error:{code:"already_answered"}}, which is why the frame carries the dialog id and no client-chosen response id.

WsClientPing.description: Connection-level liveness probe, answered immediately with `pong`. It is separate from the server-initiated heartbeat so a client behind a proxy can keep an idle connection alive without subscribing to anything.

WsClientFrame.description: Union of every frame a client may send, and the document root. The hub compiles it once at construction and validates every inbound frame against it before any handler runs; a frame that fails gets response{ok:false,error:{code:"bad_request"}} when it carries an id and is dropped otherwise, so a malformed frame can never reach a handler or tear the connection down.

piVersion.description: pi version the server was built and probed against (0.87.1 in the spike). A mismatch degrades with a clear message instead of failing mid-run.

features.description: Capability flags the server advertises. Clients degrade gracefully when a flag is missing and ignore flags they do not know; the spike advertises the subset it really implements.

limits.description: Server limits as scalars (maxSessions, replayEvents, replayWindowSec, dialogTimeoutSec, heartbeatSec, sendBuffer, ...). Open map so a new limit lands without a breaking schema change.

WsServerInfo.description: Server identity and advertised capabilities, re-declared from core.json's ServerInfo (which stays authoritative for REST). Pin the shape here so the `welcome` frame is self-describing.

heartbeatSec.description: Interval of the server-initiated `ping`, in seconds. Published so the client can size its own pong deadline and its reconnect policy instead of guessing a constant phase 4 would then have to change on both sides.

WsWelcome.description: Handshake response, sent once per connection. After it the client may subscribe; the server never sends a second `welcome`, so a client that needs to renegotiate opens a new connection.

type.description: Event name. Three namespaces: pi.* is a verbatim child record forwarded untouched, server.* is a lifecycle or diagnostic fact the server itself observed (spawned, ready, exited, crashed, heartbeat, replay.begin/end, dialog.timeout, error), ext.* is a fire-and-forget extension UI notification. A client that meets an unknown name must ignore the event, never disconnect: that is what lets the server ship new pi events without a protocol bump.

seq.description: Global, per-server-process sequence number assigned by the hub. Clients use it as the since.seq cursor; it is deliberately not per session, so one number orders every stream a client sees.

payload.description: Event body, verbatim. For pi.* events it is the child record byte for byte, including fields this server does not understand; for server.* events it is the documented per-type object.

WsEvent.description: The one frame type that carries the event stream. sessionId is absent only for server-wide facts (heartbeat, startup diagnostics), and entryId only for events that do not map to a pi session entry.

id.description: pi request id, passed through verbatim and echoed by the answering `ui_response`. The hub does not assign it: the child owns the dialog identity.

method.description: Dialog kind, copied from the child's extension_ui_request. Only the answerable methods appear here — fire-and-forget ones (notify, setStatus, setWidget, setTitle, set_editor_text) become ext.* events instead, because they must never block on a client.

title.description: Dialog title supplied by the extension, e.g. the tool name that wants approval.

message.description: Optional dialog body, e.g. the bash command awaiting approval.

options.description: Choices of a select dialog, in the order the extension supplied them.

placeholder.description: Hint text for an input dialog.

prefill.description: Initial content of an editor dialog.

timeoutMs.description: Deadline requested by the child, in milliseconds. The effective deadline is the smaller of this and the server's dialog timeout; on expiry the server answers the child with cancelled=true and publishes server.dialog.timeout.

WsRequest.description: A blocking extension UI question, broadcast to the current subscribers of the session. It is a frame of its own rather than an event because it demands an answer: the first ui_response with this id wins, so clients can render it as a prompt instead of a log line.

id.description: Correlation id copied from the frame being answered: the client-chosen id of a `command`, the pi request id of a `ui_response`, or the id of the malformed frame that produced a bad_request.

ok.description: true when the request succeeded. false always carries `error`; there is no third, ambiguous state, so a client can drop its pending-operation entry on every response it sees.

data.description: Result of a successful command, verbatim from the handler. Untyped because it is op-specific; clients type it per op and tolerate fields they do not know.

WsResponse.description: Terminal outcome of one request. Exactly one arrives per id, including for frames that failed validation, so a client never has to time out a request it sent.

WsPong.description: Answer to a `ping` or to the server heartbeat, and the only proof of liveness the hub acts on: after three consecutive heartbeats without any inbound traffic the connection is closed, so a half-open TCP connection cannot hold a subscriber slot forever.

id.description: Client-chosen id, echoed in the response frame exactly like a command id, so a client never waits for an answer it cannot correlate.

dir.description: Working directory of the shell. It is resolved through the workspace confinement before any process is started: a directory outside every root is a path_escape and no shell is spawned.

cols.description: Initial terminal width in columns. Omitted means the server default.

rows.description: Initial terminal height in rows. Omitted means the server default.

WsClientTerminalOpen.description: Opens a PTY in one workspace directory. Operator scope only: a terminal runs arbitrary commands, so it is the one read-adjacent frame that a viewer may not send. The answer is a `response` frame carrying `{terminalId, cwd, cols, rows, pid}`.

terminalId.description: Terminal the bytes go to, as the open response reported it.

data.description: Base64 of the bytes to write to the PTY, because a keystroke is bytes and a chunk may split a UTF-8 rune; a JSON string would corrupt what the shell receives.

WsClientTerminalInput.description: Writes input to an open terminal. A terminal the connection does not own is a not_found, never somebody else's shell.

WsClientTerminalResize.description: Tells the shell how big the client's terminal is. The size reaches the process as SIGWINCH, which is what makes a full-screen program redraw instead of wrapping at the wrong column.

WsClientTerminalClose.description: Closes one terminal. Idempotent: a terminal that is already gone is a successful close, because the client's intent (it is not using it any more) is satisfied either way. The whole process group is signalled, so a command the shell started does not outlive it.

data.description: Base64 of the bytes the PTY produced. It is a stream of its own: these frames carry no seq and are never replayed, because a terminal is live state and not a conversation.

WsTerminalOutput.description: Output of an open terminal, written to the connection that opened it. A terminal has exactly one reader on purpose: two clients typing into one shell is a shared session, which is a different feature with its own frames.

exitCode.description: Exit status of the shell, -1 when a signal ended it or when the exit status is unknown.

reason.description: Why it closed: `client` (the client asked), `owner` (the connection that owned it is gone), `server` (a shutdown) or `exit` (the shell ended on its own).

WsTerminalClosed.description: One terminal is gone, with the reason and the exit status. Sent exactly once per terminal, after the last output chunk, so a client can close its pane without polling.
